szoveg_eredeti:
Community Traditional Chinese Medicine Artificial Intelligence Services Lack Longitudinal Outcome Data

Community health centers deploying artificial intelligence to assist with traditional Chinese medicine services provide constitution assessments and personalized recommendations for older adults, but public records reveal that systematic follow-up procedures and longitudinal health outcome evaluations remain largely undocumented. An exploratory policy and practice review conducted by Sitong Wu from The Fifth Clinical Medical College at Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine analyzed public materials from three municipal and county programs across China to investigate how continuing care is structured after an initial diagnostic check. The investigation examined community initiatives operating in Shenzhen, Hefei, and Taihe County, evaluating publicly available descriptions against a structured five-dimension analytical framework. While every examined program reported using digital algorithms to determine a resident’s traditional Chinese medicine constitution type and issue tailored lifestyle guidance, none of the analyzed public sources provided systematic longitudinal health-outcome data specific to older adult populations, exposing critical evidence gaps between initial technological evaluations and sustained clinical management.

The integration of digital health innovations into grassroots healthcare occurs alongside major demographic transitions in mainland China, where aging populations increasingly require coordinated, person-centered long-term care. National population sample survey data gathered in November 2025 indicated that 321.22 million citizens were aged 60 years or older, representing 22.86 percent of the country’s population, while 223.09 million individuals were aged 65 years or older, comprising 15.87 percent of the national total. Guidelines established by the World Health Organization regarding integrated care for older people emphasize coordinating health assessments, personalized interventions, and ongoing clinical management around individual functional capacity. Within China’s institutional landscape, the National Basic Public Health Service Program already delivers standardized traditional Chinese medicine health management to permanent residents aged 65 and above through neighborhood health centers and township clinics. Under this established national public scheme, primary healthcare workers conduct mandatory annual constitution identification assessments classifying older adults into nine formal constitution categories and deliver individualized lifestyle guidance covering nutrition, daily habits, emotional balance, physical exercise, and acupoint care.

Despite wide geographic coverage, the conventional annual management model faces operational hurdles, including a twelve-month gap between evaluations, severe personnel constraints among primary care practitioners, and evaluation standards centered on delivery completion rather than long-term adherence or functional health outcomes. To augment these services, grassroots centers have increasingly piloted artificial intelligence diagnostic tools that capture facial images, analyze tongue characteristics, and process intelligent clinical questionnaires to identify body constitutions. Although computational algorithms offer efficiency, digital accessibility, and automated record-keeping capabilities, current community deployments typically operate as isolated pilot projects rather than systems formally embedded in statutory public health workflows. When novel technologies merely deliver a single assessment and generate recommendations without established mechanisms for continuing care, practitioners cannot verify whether older residents execute prescribed regimens, encounter adverse effects, or experience measurable improvements over time.

To rigorously examine public accounts of these emerging services, the review gathered source documents across 2026, including government project releases, technology vendor reports, and professional medical journalism. The author applied an analytical framework built around five sequential operational phases: health assessment, individualized recommendations, task execution monitoring, reassessment and outcome evaluation, and regimen adjustment. The analysis employed the concept of observability from Everett Rogers’ diffusion of innovations theory as a sensitizing lens to explore how clearly programs document processes and observable outcomes. Observability addresses the degree to which an innovation’s results are visible to participants and external observers. The review emphasized that analyzing public documentation serves an interpretive purpose and does not measure actual user trust, perceived observability, patient compliance, or clinical efficacy. Furthermore, public disclosures reflect varying promotional or reporting objectives rather than independently audited health service research, requiring strict separation between stated software features, confirmed field implementations, and independently validated health results.

A granular examination of the three local cases illustrated divergent levels of reporting detail across the service pathway. In Shenzhen’s Dalang Subdistrict, the Silver-Age Health Cabin initiative launched across community older-adult centers in May 2025 utilized digital facial and tongue image capture to generate constitution reports alongside dietary and acupoint advice, recording 572 non-unique service encounters across 16 activities by September 2025; however, the project documents detailed separate psychological companionship robots and virtual reality devices rather than ongoing monitoring of the traditional regimens. In Hefei’s Wannianbu Subdistrict Community Health Service Center, system vendor reports described automated facial and tongue assessments paired with digital questionnaires, documenting repeated assessments for a single individual while identifying the creation of a routine follow-up mechanism only as an unfulfilled future objective. In Taihe County’s Yinxing Community Health Service Center, media reports described diagnostic pulse and tongue devices supporting constitution assessment and prescription generation, alongside chronic disease follow-up, health check-in functions, return-visit reminders, and regimen adjustments, but without detailing eligibility criteria, verification rules, or separate statistics for older residents.

A synthesis of cross-case findings revealed consistent adoption of artificial intelligence at the intake stage but persistent gaps in operational accountability throughout subsequent stages of care. While all three initiatives documented algorithm-assisted constitution classification and individualized lifestyle recommendations, none provided systematic, longitudinal outcome measurements demonstrating clinical benefit or functional stability among older adults. Incomplete reporting was particularly pronounced regarding routine verification rules for daily health behaviors, standardized instruments for follow-up evaluation, and systematic protocols governing clinical regimen modifications. Descriptions of check-ins or software notifications did not establish whether tasks were performed correctly, nor did institutional assertions confirm verified health improvements. The review cautioned that missing details in public reports do not prove that continuing services are completely absent in daily practice, but the absence of verified documentation prevents independent assessment of program efficacy and highlights an urgent need for rigorous empirical field evaluations.

Addressing the disconnect between digital assessments and routine community practice, the author formulated a testable adherence-support framework designed to integrate into China’s existing public health infrastructure.
